Two antennas radiate weak radio fields, and the performer's hands, moving in the air beside them, alter pitch and volume by changing the capacitance of the circuit. Because nothing in the empty air marks where one note ends and the next begins, the instrument offers a player no _____, and every pitch has to be found by ear alone.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: Ndebele women paint the outer walls of their houses in blocks of saturated colour bounded by black lines, working freehand with a chicken feather and no drawn guide. A wall is repainted after each rainy season, and a painter will alter the design rather than copy the last one exactly. The practice the wall records is therefore continuous without being _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The bombardier beetle stores hydrogen peroxide in one chamber and hydroquinone in another and keeps the two apart until something threatens it. Mixed over a catalyst in a third chamber, they react and are fired out at the temperature of boiling water. Keeping the ingredients _____ until the instant of use is what lets the animal carry a weapon that would otherwise destroy the body holding it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The English Exchequer recorded a debt by notching a hazel stick across its width and then splitting it lengthwise, so that creditor and debtor each kept a half. The grain of any given stick runs in a way no other stick repeats, so the two halves fit each other and nothing else. Since a forged half would fail the simplest test there is, the system was remarkably _____.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “ground” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Before an etcher touches the copper, the plate is covered with a thin acid-resistant coating of wax and resin and smoked black so that the lines will show. The needle takes this coating away wherever it passes, and when the plate goes into the bath the acid bites only where the <u>ground</u> has been cleared.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The background against which a figure is seen.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Solid earth at the surface of the land.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A protective coating laid on a plate before it is etched.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A reason offered in support of a claim.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A drawing does not move. Set a strip of drawings inside a slotted drum and spin it, and an eye at the slots sees each drawing for an instant and the wall of the drum between them. The gaps matter as much as the pictures: without them the images would smear into one another and nothing would appear to move at all. What the device supplies is not motion but the interruption that lets a sequence of stills read as motion.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It compares the zoetrope with the motion-picture cameras that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It traces the invention of the zoetrope through its several patents.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It argues that the human eye is easily deceived by rapid images.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It states a limitation, describes a device that appears to overcome it, and identifies what the device actually contributes.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Along some rivers in Thailand whole bankside trees of fireflies flash in unison, and the rhythm holds for hours. <u>Each insect shifts its own cycle a little earlier or later whenever it sees a neighbour flash, and a population of insects doing only that settles into a common beat with none of them leading.</u> Searches for a conductor among the flashing beetles have all failed, because there is nothing of the kind to find.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It questions whether the flashing is genuinely synchronised.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It describes the habitat in which the fireflies gather.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It reports the outcome of a search for a leading insect.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It supplies the mechanism that accounts for the coordination described, and that the final sentence depends on.

questions.stem: According to the text, why did locally kept time become unworkable?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Before 1883 a town in the United States kept whatever time its own noon gave it, and a traveller crossing the country reset a watch dozens of times. That was tolerable at the speed of a horse. It was not tolerable on a railway, where two trains sharing one track are held apart by a timetable, and a timetable is worthless if the two crews are working to different clocks. The railway companies, not the government, cut the country into four zones and imposed them on 18 November 1883; the law caught up thirty-five years later.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Astronomers could not agree among themselves on when noon occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Travellers found resetting their watches at every town inconvenient.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Trains sharing a track were kept apart by timetables that required every crew to keep the same clock.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The federal government required a single national standard from 1883.

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the main advantage of the floats over ship-based measurement?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An Argo float sinks to two kilometres, drifts with the current for ten days, descends further, then rises to the surface measuring temperature and salinity as it climbs and radios the profile to a satellite before sinking again. Four thousand of them work the open ocean. Before the programme, most subsurface measurements came from ships, which meant they came from shipping lanes, in summer, in the northern hemisphere. The floats do not measure more accurately than a ship does; they measure where no ship goes.

choices.label: A
choices.content: They sample parts of the ocean and times of year that ships rarely reach.

choices.label: B
choices.content: They are considerably cheaper to build than a research vessel.

choices.label: C
choices.content: They can remain at the surface indefinitely without maintenance.

choices.label: D
choices.content: They record temperature and salinity more precisely than shipboard instruments do.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitcombe's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Fewer than a hundred Wollemi pines survive in a canyon west of Sydney, and the species was known only from fossils until 1994. Botanist Ngaire Whitcombe argues that the surviving trees amount to a single individual, propagated by shoots from the base rather than from seed.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Fossil pollen of the genus is found across Australia and Antarctica.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The steep walls of the canyon have sheltered the grove from fire.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Sequencing of trees taken from every part of the grove finds no detectable genetic variation between them.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The trees bear both male and female cones on the same individual.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Boateng's argument over the alternative?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A gecko walks up a pane of glass. Its toes carry millions of hairs, each splitting into finer tips, and the pads leave no residue behind. Physicist Amara Boateng argues that the adhesion comes from van der Waals attraction between those tips and the surface rather than from suction.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Some spiders and beetles also carry adhesive hairs on their feet.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Geckos adhere just as strongly inside a chamber pumped down to a near-vacuum, where there is no surrounding air to be excluded from beneath the pads.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A gecko's toes peel away from the surface tip first when it lifts a foot.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Gecko pads adhere better to smooth surfaces than to rough ones.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Corrigan's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A platypus dives with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut and finds shrimp in muddy water. Its bill carries tens of thousands of pores, some sensitive to touch and some to weak electric fields. Zoologist Elspeth Corrigan argues that the animal locates prey by combining the two kinds of pore rather than by relying on either alone.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The electrically sensitive pores are concentrated along the front edge of the bill.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Muscle contractions in a shrimp generate electric fields strong enough to detect.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A platypus strikes accurately at a battery-driven electrode only when a pressure wave reaches the bill at the same moment, and misses when either signal is presented on its own.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A sundial reads the sun; a clock reads an average. The Earth's orbit is elliptical, so the planet moves faster along it in January than in July, and the tilt of the axis changes how the sun's daily motion projects onto the dial. Taken together the two effects put solar noon as much as sixteen minutes away from clock noon at some times of year and bring the two together at others. An accurate clock and a well-made sundial will therefore agree _____

choices.label: C
choices.content: at every time of year, once the dial has been correctly aligned.

choices.label: D
choices.content: on only a few dates in the year.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A charge for driving into a city centre at peak hours reduces the number of cars entering it. The drivers who stop coming are by definition those who valued the trip at less than the charge. Which trips those are depends on what else is available: someone whose route is served by a frequent train has an easy substitute, while someone starting at four in the morning from an outer suburb may have none. Introduced without any improvement to those alternatives, such a charge falls hardest on _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: drivers with the fewest other ways of making the trip.

choices.label: B
choices.content: residents of the city centre itself.

choices.label: C
choices.content: commercial deliveries made during the working day.

choices.label: D
choices.content: drivers making the most valuable trips.

questions.passage: Rafflesia has no leaves, no stem and no roots of its own; it lives as threads inside a jungle vine and shows itself only as a flower a metre across. Because the plant spends all but a few days of its life entirely hidden inside its _____ working in Sumatra map the vines rather than the flowers.

questions.passage: A suminagashi print is lifted off the surface of a bath of still water. The maker touches the water alternately with a brush of ink and a brush of surfactant so that each ring spreads inside the last, then lays down a sheet of absorbent _____ up the whole pattern in a single contact and cannot be laid down twice.

John Roebling's mill at Trenton twisted fine wires into strands and the strands into _____ so made bends around a sheave, and a broken wire inside it can be found and replaced without taking the whole thing down.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A ferrofluid is a suspension of iron oxide grains a few nanometres across, each one coated so that the grains cannot clump together. The liquid pours like any other with no magnet _____ a field held beneath the dish draws the surface up into a bed of spikes that stand while the magnet is there and collapse the moment it is taken away.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The network reports continuously, and a station that falls silent for more than an hour brings a technician up the mountain. Each of the seven seismographs on the flank _____ its own battery, a solar panel and a radio link back to the observatory.

questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two gauges of the same pattern were read every morning for thirty years, one on the escarpment and one in the town below it. The rainfall recorded at the upland gauge is nearly double _____ recorded at the gauge in the town.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

The wildlife trust has spent a decade putting bends back into two of them. This brook is one of the few chalk streams in the district that _____ never been dredged or realigned.

questions.passage: Scores on standardised intelligence tests rose in every country that kept records through the twentieth century, and the tests were periodically made harder so that the average would come back to a hundred. _____ the number such a test reports is set by comparison with the current population rather than against any fixed standard.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An electric car slows itself by running its motor backwards as a generator, returning some of the energy of motion to the battery instead of throwing it away as heat. _____ every such car is still built with friction brakes, because a generator cannot hold a stationary vehicle on a hill and loses its grip entirely as the wheels stop turning.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A dancer trained in bharatanatyam tells a story with the hands, and the vocabulary of hand positions is fixed: the same shape carries the same meaning for any audience that knows the form. _____ a passage of the dance can be followed by someone sitting too far back to see the dancer's face, provided the hands are held clear of the body.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise an obstacle to changing school start times. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Adolescent sleep timing shifts later at puberty for biological reasons.
  • Many secondary schools begin before eight in the morning.
  • A district in Minneapolis moved its high school start from 7.15 to 8.40 in 1997.
  • Attendance rose and reported sleep on school nights increased by about an hour.
  • Bus fleets are shared between primary and secondary schools, so one timetable constrains the other.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A district in Minneapolis moved its high school start from 7.15 to 8.40 in 1997, and attendance rose.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Although the Minneapolis change raised attendance and added about an hour of sleep on school nights, bus fleets shared between primary and secondary schools mean that one timetable constrains the other.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Reported sleep on school nights increased by about an hour after the Minneapolis change.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Adolescent sleep timing shifts later at puberty for biological reasons.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the material can be gathered only at certain times of year. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Bark for painting is cut from the stringybark eucalyptus only in the wet season, when it will lift from the trunk.
  • The sheet is warmed over a fire and weighted flat for several weeks.
  • Pigments are ochres ground on stone and bound with the sap of an orchid.
  • Paintings collected in the 1940s were catalogued as artefacts rather than as works by named artists.
  • Museums have since re-attributed many of them to individual painters.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Paintings collected in the 1940s were catalogued as artefacts rather than as works by named artists.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Bark will lift from the stringybark eucalyptus only in the wet season, which is when sheets for painting are cut.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A bark sheet is warmed over a fire and weighted flat for several weeks before it is painted.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Pigments are ochres ground on stone and bound with the sap of an orchid.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how a single singer produces two lines at once. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In khoomei a singer produces a low drone and a whistling melody at the same time.
  • The drone is a single note produced at the vocal folds.
  • The melody is made of harmonics already present in that drone.
  • Changing the shape of the mouth and tongue amplifies one harmonic at a time.
  • A listener hears two voices although only one note is being sung.

choices.label: A
choices.content: In khoomei a singer produces a low drone and a whistling melody at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A listener hears two voices although only one note is being sung.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The melody is not a second note but a harmonic of the drone, picked out one at a time by changes in the shape of the mouth and tongue.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The drone in khoomei is a single note produced at the vocal folds.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A wycinanki maker folds a sheet of paper once and cuts through both halves in a single stroke, so the finished cockerel or spruce is identical on either side of the fold. The tool is a pair of sheep shears, held in one hand and worked against paper turned by the other. The symmetry of the result is neither drawn nor measured; it is _____ by the method itself.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Deaf children brought together at a school in Managua in the late 1970s had no language in common: each arrived with gestures invented at home. Within a few years the older pupils were signing fluently to one another, and the youngest, who learned from them, produced a grammar more regular than anything the first cohort had used. The language was not taught to them; it _____ among them.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “stops” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An organ is not one instrument but many. Each rank of pipes has a timbre of its own, and the player admits wind to a rank by drawing the knob that governs it; drawing several at once blends their voices into a single sound. A large instrument may offer sixty such <u>stops</u>, and no two organs are laid out alike.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Places where a vehicle halts to take on passengers.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Sets of pipes of one timbre, together with the controls that bring them into play.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Obstructions placed inside a pipe to block the flow of air.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Periods during which an activity is suspended.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The trigonometrical survey of India began with a baseline measured on the plain south of Madras with steel chains laid end to end. Every later distance in the chain of triangles was computed from that one line rather than paced out, so an error in it would have propagated through the entire network. The accuracy of everything downstream was _____ on a single measurement, which is why the baseline was remeasured again and again.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Trawlers working the southern North Sea bring up peat, freshwater shells and worked flint along with the fish. The ground beneath them was dry until about eight thousand years ago, when rising seas closed over a plain that had joined Britain to the continent. What the nets recover is therefore not rubbish washed out from the shore but a landscape _____ where its people left it.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: In 1806 Frederic Tudor shipped 130 tons of pond ice from Boston to Martinique and lost most of the cargo and all of his money. The trouble was not the voyage but the storage at the far end. Over the next two decades he built insulated icehouses in the ports he sold to, packed the cargo in sawdust from the mills of Maine, and gave chilled drinks away until a taste for them existed. By 1850 ice was among the largest exports leaving Massachusetts.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To argue that the ice trade was more profitable than the timber trade.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To recount the history of imports into Martinique in the nineteenth century.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To describe how a failed venture was made viable by changes in storage and in demand.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To explain the physics by which sawdust insulates a block of ice.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Bar-headed geese cross the Himalaya on migration, flying where the air holds about a third of the oxygen available at sea level. <u>Their haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than that of lowland geese, and the capillaries in their flight muscle run closer to the fibres they supply.</u> Birds flown in a chamber with the oxygen reduced to match those heights keep beating their wings at a rate a lowland goose cannot sustain for a minute.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It identifies the physiological features that account for the performance reported elsewhere in the text.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It describes the route the geese follow across the mountains.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It questions whether the geese fly as high as has been reported.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It explains how the oxygen level in the chamber was reduced.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The gold tesserae of a Byzantine apse are not laid flat. Each cube of glass with its leaf of gold is pressed into the setting bed at a slight angle to its neighbours, and the angles vary across the surface. A wall set that way never returns the same reflection twice: as a visitor moves, different cubes catch the light from the windows and the gold seems to travel across the vault. Set flush, the same material gives one hard glare and nothing moves.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Byzantine mosaicists worked more slowly than their Roman predecessors.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The apse was the most difficult part of a Byzantine church to decorate.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The gold used in Byzantine wall mosaics was of unusually high purity.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Setting the tesserae at varying angles makes the reflected light shift as the viewer moves.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Ramps cut into the kerb at street corners were won by disabled campaigners in Berkeley in the 1970s over objections that the expense would serve very few people. Counts taken at intersections afterwards found that most of those using the ramps were pushing prams, wheeling luggage or delivery trolleys, or riding bicycles. The ramps had not created these users. The users had been lifting and dragging.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Objections to the ramps were based mainly on how they would look.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Most people using kerb ramps today are wheelchair users.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The ramps proved to serve far more people than the group who campaigned for them.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Berkeley was the first city in the United States to install ramps of this kind.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Wenzel's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The man found in a glacier on the Italian-Austrian border in 1991 carried an axe with a blade of nearly pure copper. Because the Alpine copper workings known at the time are later than his radiocarbon date, several accounts have him carrying metal traded up from the Balkans. Archaeometallurgist Petra Wenzel argues instead that the copper was smelted from ore close to where he died.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The lead isotope ratios in the blade match those of ore bodies in the southern Alps within a few days' walk of the find, and not those of Balkan ores.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Copper axes of similar shape have been found across central Europe.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The haft of the axe is yew, a wood available throughout the Alps.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Balkan copper of the period is known to have been traded over long distances.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nakamura's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: In 1860 Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville traced sound onto soot-blackened paper with a stylus attached to a membrane. He built no way of playing the tracings back and said he had never intended one. Historian Ruth Nakamura argues that the phonautograph was designed as an instrument for studying the shapes of speech rather than as a failed attempt at recorded sound.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Scott worked as a typesetter and had access to printed accounts of acoustics.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Edison's phonograph, which could play sound back, appeared seventeen years later.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Scott's notebooks pair his tracings with the vowels being spoken and compare their shapes, and he petitioned for the device to be adopted in the teaching of shorthand.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Modern software has reconstructed audible sound from Scott's surviving tracings.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Halvorsen's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Late-summer snowfields in the Arctic turn pink where algae bloom in the melting surface layer, and the same fields have been photographed from the air every August since the 1970s. Clean snow returns most of the sunlight that falls on it, while a pigmented surface takes more of that light in as heat. Glaciologist Tomas Halvorsen argues that these blooms are themselves a significant cause of the melting rather than merely a symptom of it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plots in which the algae were suppressed reflected about a seventh more sunlight across the season and lost measurably less depth than untreated plots beside them.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Blooms appear earlier in years when the spring is warm.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Algae of the same kind are found on snowfields on four continents.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Pigmented algal cells survive the winter frozen into the snowpack.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A barnacle glues itself to rock that is already wet, and its cement sets under water. Ordinary adhesives fail there because a film of water sits between the glue and the surface and neither will bond through it. Analysis of a settling larva shows that its first secretion is an oily phase that spreads out ahead of the cement. The purpose of that oily phase is therefore most likely to _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: shield the cement from predators while it sets.

choices.label: B
choices.content: harden into the bond that holds the animal down.

choices.label: C
choices.content: displace the water film so that the cement can reach the surface.

choices.label: D
choices.content: dissolve the outer layer of the rock beneath it.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A zeolite is an aluminosilicate whose crystal structure is riddled with channels of a single fixed width. Molecules narrower than the channel pass in and are held; molecules wider than it cannot enter at all. The width does not change with temperature or pressure in the way a filter's pores might. To separate one gas from another with such a material, then, an engineer has to choose a zeolite whose channels are _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: intermediate in width between the two molecules.

choices.label: B
choices.content: narrower than both of the molecules involved.

choices.label: C
choices.content: able to widen as the gas is heated.

choices.label: D
choices.content: wider than either of the two molecules to be separated.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A netsuke is the toggle that stops a cord from slipping through a sash, and it is handled constantly, so it can carry no sharp projection anywhere on it. The carver Kaigyokusai Masatsugu, a man who worked in ivory and boxwood in nineteenth-century _____ his figures so that every limb folds back into the mass of the piece.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The ship buried at Oseberg in 834 was already old when it went into the ground, and its timbers were carved along every visible edge. Blue clay and a cap of turf sealed the mound and kept the air out of _____ wood, the textiles and a wooden cart came out of it in a condition no ordinary grave would have left them in.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why place-names are useful evidence for settlement. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Place-names ending in -by and -thorpe are Old Norse in origin.
  • Names ending in -ton and -ham are Old English.
  • The Norse endings are dense in Lincolnshire and Yorkshire and rare in Devon.
  • Written records of Scandinavian settlement in England are thin and were made by hostile chroniclers.
  • Names stay attached to the land through changes of ownership.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because written accounts of the settlement are thin and hostile, historians turn to names, which stay attached to the land through changes of ownership and so map where Norse speakers settled.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Written records of Scandinavian settlement in England are thin and were made by hostile chroniclers.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Place-names ending in -by and -thorpe are Old Norse, while those ending in -ton and -ham are Old English.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The Norse endings are dense in Lincolnshire and Yorkshire and rare in Devon.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how the device kept the outcome from being fixed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

  • Citizens' name tokens were slotted into the columns; black and white balls were fed into the tube.
  • Each ball drawn selected or rejected a whole row of tokens at once.
  • The order of the balls could not be known in advance.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Citizens' name tokens were slotted into the columns of the slab.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A kleroterion was a stone slab with columns of slots and a tube down one side.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Most Athenian public offices in the fourth century BCE were filled by lot rather than by election.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Because each ball drawn took or rejected a whole row of name tokens and the order of the balls could not be known beforehand, no official could arrange which citizens were chosen.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise how quickly the service was made obsolete. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

  • The transcontinental telegraph line was completed on 24 October 1861.
  • The Pony Express announced its closure two days later.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A service that had opened in April 1860 announced its closure two days after the transcontinental telegraph was completed in October 1861.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The transcontinental telegraph line was completed on 24 October 1861.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A letter carried by the Pony Express cost five dollars a half-ounce at the start of the service.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The Pony Express used around 180 relay stations and 400 horses to carry mail from Missouri to California.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.content: It explains why glass is chosen for the bead rather than another material.

choices.label: B

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.content: To trace the history of the vacuum valve from its invention onward.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raghavan's argument?

questions.passage: An ant infected by the fungus Ophiocordyceps leaves its nest, climbs a sapling and clamps its jaws onto a leaf vein about twenty-five centimetres above the ground before it dies; the fungus then fruits from the back of its head. choices.content: Infected ants have been found on the leaves of many different species of sapling.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The fungus can be grown on a laboratory medium with no insect host at all.

choices.content: Uninfected ants sometimes climb saplings in the course of ordinary foraging.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Fungi that fruited on ants moved to other heights released spores that infected far fewer ants than those released at about twenty-five centimetres, where humidity and temperature best suit the fungus.

questions.passage: Under a ranked ballot a candidate who cannot win outright may still gain from being placed second by a rival's supporters. choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.content: Turnout is slightly higher in ranked-ballot elections than in plurality elections.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain what the toughness of the silk is needed for. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: B
choices.content: Caerostris darwini spins webs across rivers in Madagascar, some of them spanning twenty-five metres.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A bridging line stretched twenty-five metres over a river has to absorb the impact of insects struck at speed above open water, which is what this spider's unusually tough dragline silk allows.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The spider releases a line into the wind and waits for it to catch on the far bank.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.content: In 1935 about one farm in ten in the United States had electric power.

questions.stem: A sculptor casts a small bronze maquette that uses 350 cubic centimetres of bronze, then casts a finished statue similar to the maquette with every dimension 3 times as large. How many cubic centimetres of bronze does the finished statue use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rainwater butt is a right circular cylinder whose base has an area of 1,800 square centimetres. The butt holds 27 litres of water, and 1 litre is 1,000 cubic centimetres. What is the depth of the water in the butt, in centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A courier works out the fee for a parcel, in dollars, as \(5x-13\), where x is the mass of the parcel in kilograms. The fee for one parcel came to $42. What was that parcel's mass, in kilograms?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: At a harbour market, mackerel costs $4 a kilogram and squid costs $9 a kilogram. A chef bought 5 kilograms of mackerel together with some squid and spent $65 in all. How many kilograms of squid did the chef buy?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A lighthouse keeper's logbook has 260 blank pages at the start of a season, and 3 of those pages are filled in each day. Which expression gives the number of blank pages left after d days?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A tram network sets the fare for a journey by the rule \(C(k)=1.80+0.45k\), where k is the length of the journey in kilometres and \(C(k)\) is the fare in dollars. What is the best interpretation of 1.80 in this model?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: The number of kilometres that a fare of $1.80 covers.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The fare, in dollars, charged for each kilometre travelled.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The total fare, in dollars, for a journey of 45 kilometres.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The fixed charge, in dollars, that applies to every journey however long it is.

questions.stem: A gallery will hang an open show only if no more than 40 works are submitted. Which inequality gives all the possible numbers w of submitted works for which the show is hung?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: One third of the seats in a village cinema are in the balcony. The cinema has 42 balcony seats. How many seats does the cinema have altogether?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A church candle stands 30 centimetres tall when it is lit and burns down 2.5 centimetres in each hour that it is alight. How tall is the candle, in centimetres, after it has been alight for 6 hours?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A joiner cuts \(5m+8\) dowels for the frame of a cabinet and \(3m-2\) dowels for its shelves, where m is the number of shelves. Which expression gives the total number of dowels the joiner cuts?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A mosaic border has an area of \(6y^{2}-15y\) square centimetres, where y is its width in centimetres. Which expression is equivalent to that area?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A toboggan run's drag index is modelled by \(D(v)=v^{2}-3\), where v is the toboggan's speed in metres per second. What is the drag index at a speed of 7 metres per second?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A colony of mites doubles in size every hour, so after x hours the colony is \(2^{x}\) times as large as it was at the start. After how many hours is the colony 64 times as large as it was at the start?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The illuminance from a lamp d metres away, in lux, is modelled by \(L(d)=\frac{144}{d^{2}}\). What is the illuminance 4 metres from the lamp?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A stage crew's setup time, in minutes, is \(4(2p-3)+5p\), where p is the number of platforms being built. Which expression is equivalent to that setup time?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A struck tuning fork has an amplitude, in micrometres, of \(A(h)=80\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{h}\) after h seconds. What is the amplitude 3 seconds after the fork is struck?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A dyer's recipe calls for 3 parts woad to 5 parts water by volume. One batch made to this recipe uses 45 litres of water. How many litres of woad does that batch use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A cycle shop's stock of helmets fell from 250 helmets to 210 helmets during one month. By what percent did the stock fall?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The lengths, in centimetres, of the seven pike caught during a river survey were 42, 55, 61, 38, 74, 50 and 66. What is the median of these seven lengths, in centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A straight garden path runs into a long straight wall, meeting it at a single point and making two angles with the wall. One of those two angles measures 63°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the other angle?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An ornamental pond is a circle of radius 9 metres. What is the area of the pond, in square metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A shipping crate is a rectangular prism measuring 4 feet long, 3 feet wide and 5 feet tall. What is the volume of the crate, in cubic feet?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A carpenter stiffens a right-angled corner with a straight diagonal batten. The two arms of the corner measure 9 centimetres and 12 centimetres. How many centimetres long is the batten?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Two balance conditions in a chemical process are written as \(6x-4y=14\) and \(9x+ky=21\), where k is a constant. Every pair \((x,y)\) that satisfies the first condition also satisfies the second. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A pressure transducer's calibration is a linear function f that turns a raw count into a corrected reading. The calibration record shows \(f(-1)=11\) and \(f(5)=-7\). What is the value of \(f(9)\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A joinery makes stools and benches from the same stock of oak. Each stool uses 3 board-feet of oak and each bench uses 8 board-feet, and at most 240 board-feet are available. The joinery must also make at least 3 times as many stools as benches. What is the greatest number of benches the joinery can make?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A tug leaves a jetty and travels along a straight channel at a constant 14 kilometres per hour. Two hours later a launch leaves the same jetty along the same channel at a constant 21 kilometres per hour. How many kilometres from the jetty does the launch draw level with the tug?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A haulier charges $95 for the first 40 kilometres of any delivery and a fixed amount for each kilometre beyond the first 40. A delivery of 130 kilometres costs $455. How many dollars does a delivery of 200 kilometres cost?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A market stall's takings satisfy \(3a+5c=41\) and \(5a+3c=47\), where a is the price in dollars of an apron and c is the price in dollars of a cushion. What is the combined price, in dollars, of one apron and one cushion?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A kiln must be held at a temperature of at least 940 degrees Celsius and at most 1,060 degrees Celsius. The controller reading r and the temperature T, in degrees Celsius, are related by \(T=25r+540\). Which inequality gives every controller reading r that holds the kiln in the required range?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A calibration routine for a densitometer uses the two functions \(q(z)=z^{2}-2\) and \(p(z)=az+7\), where a is a constant. Feeding the reading 3 into q and then feeding the result of that into p produces 35. What is the value of a?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An optics model gives the effective gain of a lens stack as \(\frac{2x^{2}-18}{x^{2}+6x+9}\), where \(x>0\). Which expression is equivalent to that gain?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The floor of a tunnel has the profile \(y=x^{2}-6x+13\), and a survey laser is set at the constant height \(y=k\), with x and y in metres. The laser meets the floor profile at exactly one point. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rectangular allotment plot is 7 metres longer than it is wide and covers 330 square metres. What is the perimeter of the plot, in metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A materials index is recorded as \(\frac{\left(27b^{6}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}}}{9b^{5}}\), where \(b>0\). Which expression is equivalent to that index?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The height of a suspended footbridge cable above the deck is modelled by \(s(x)=\frac{1}{50}(x-30)^{2}+c\) metres, where x is the distance in metres from one tower and c is a constant. The cable is 20 metres above the deck at \(x=0\). How many metres above the deck is the cable at \(x=50\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A culture of yeast triples in mass every 5 hours, and its mass is 12 grams at the moment the culture is started. Which function gives the mass of the culture, in grams, t hours after it is started?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The mean mass of the 14 salmon held in one tank of a hatchery is 4.2 kilograms, and the mean mass of the 6 salmon held in a second tank is 5.7 kilograms. What is the mean mass, in kilograms, of all 20 salmon?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A conveyor delivers crushed stone into a wagon at a constant 45 kilograms per minute. The wagon holds 13.5 tonnes of stone, and 1 tonne is 1,000 kilograms. How many hours does the conveyor take to fill the wagon?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A researcher measured the wingspan of each of 60 randomly selected gulls from a colony of 900 gulls and found that 21 of the selected gulls had a wingspan of more than 140 centimetres. Based on this sample, how many of the 900 gulls would be estimated to have a wingspan of more than 140 centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A trestle frame is built in the shape of triangle \(ABC\), with a cross-brace \(DE\) joining a point D on \(AB\) to a point E on \(AC\) so that \(DE\) is parallel to \(BC\). The brace divides \(AB\) so that \(AD=6\) feet and \(DB=9\) feet, and the brace itself is 8 feet long. What is the length, in feet, of \(BC\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A grain hopper is a right circular cylinder of radius 3 metres and height 5 metres with a cone of the same radius and of height 4 metres fixed on top of it. What is the total volume of the hopper, in cubic metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A draughtsman's set square is a right triangle \(LMN\) whose right angle is at N. The leg \(LN\) measures 24 centimetres and the leg \(MN\) measures 7 centimetres. What is the value of \(\cos L\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A solid metal cube whose edges are 10 centimetres long is melted down and recast, with no metal lost, into a single solid rectangular block measuring 25 centimetres by 8 centimetres by h centimetres. What is the value of h?
questions.subject: MATH
